title: Stranger Things — Main Title
take: Huge hollow glowing letter outlines drift past in close-up and slowly lock into one title
breakdown: Winner of the 2017 Emmy for Outstanding Main Title Design and a title made of nothing but type: for most of its ~50 seconds the camera passes in macro over the edges of hollow, glowing letters, and only at the end do they settle into the full title. It works because the viewer reads shape and light long before reading the word, so the reveal feels earned. To use it: set a short word in a heavy display face as outlines only, add a glow (stacked blurred copies of the stroke), start zoomed in 5–6× with each letter offset sideways on its own layer, and drift everything slowly and linearly to register while pulling back; no cuts, no bounce.

title: Material Design — introduction film
take: A circle of new colour or content grows from the touch point until it fills the surface
breakdown: The 49-second film that introduced Material Design at Google I/O 2014; the circular reveal it shows (at about 0:13, 0:19, 0:27 and 0:42) later shipped as a platform API in Android 5.0. It works because the change starts exactly where the finger is, so cause and effect are one gesture and the eye never has to hunt. To use it: stack the new state under a circular clip-path centred on the touch point and grow the radius until it covers the surface (0.4–0.5 s, fast out, slow in); fade the touch dot as the circle leaves it.

title: 200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes
take: Bubbles drift across a fixed chart while a giant year ticks up behind them
breakdown: The best-known animated chart ever broadcast (BBC Four, The Joy of Stats, 2010): the axes, colours and sizes never change, time is the only variable, and the year sits behind the plot as a huge watermark. It works because one encoding is held still, so every movement is data. To use it: fix the axes, map one category to colour and one quantity to radius, move every bubble at constant (linear) speed along its own path, and drive a large low-contrast year counter from the same clock; resist camera moves and gridlines.

title: iOS 26: Introducing Liquid Glass
take: Slider thumb swells into a clear glass lens that bends and magnifies what is under it
breakdown: Apple's 2025 launch film for its software redesign; the refracting control it shows (around 1:56, with a related loupe near 1:34) became the most-rebuilt UI effect of the year. It works because the control is made of the content beneath it: pressing it does not cover the track, it magnifies it. To use it: on press, spring the thumb into a larger clear capsule with a bright inner rim and a soft highlight; inside it draw a second copy of what is underneath, scaled up about 1.3× from the capsule centre and pushed outward near the edges; release with a slight overshoot.

title: Google, evolved
take: Wordmark collapses into four coloured dots that turn into bouncing equaliser bars
breakdown: The launch film for Google's 2015 identity, which made motion a state of the logo itself: the wordmark reduces to four dots that idle, listen, think and reply (about 1:14–1:50). It works because the brand keeps its colours and rhythm at any size, down to four pixels on a watch. To use it: give your mark a reduced state of a few dots, move letters into them along short arcs, idle them as a travelling wave, and stretch each dot vertically into a rounded bar whose height follows the voice; reverse the same moves to return.

title: Psycho — Main Title
take: Parallel bars sweep in, bring sliced bands of type into register, then pull them apart
breakdown: Saul Bass's 1960 sequence, built from nothing but bars and sans-serif type on black, is the textbook origin of kinetic typography in film: every credit is ushered in and escorted out by the same sliding bars. It works because the type is physically cut by the system that moves it, which makes plain words feel unstable. To use it: slice a line of bold condensed capitals into three horizontal bands with clip-paths, send each band in from a different side riding a set of evenly spaced bars at linear speed, hold in register for under a second, then pull the bands apart again.

title: Powers of Ten
take: Non-stop zoom-out where a square marks each ×10 step and an exponent counter ticks up
breakdown: Selected for the US National Film Registry in 1998, this is the origin of the continuous scale zoom that every 'cosmic zoom' explainer has copied (the outward journey runs from about 0:45 to 4:50). It works because the speed in powers is constant: each ×10 takes the same time, a square shows the next step before you reach it, and a counter names where you are. To use it: nest illustrations so each contains the previous one at its exact centre at one-tenth scale, scale exponentially (constant ratio per second), outline the next ×10 area with a thin square, and tick an exponent label as each square reaches the frame edge.

title: San Francisco Symphony — Motion Branding
take: Each letter of a serif wordmark stretches to its own height, like a waveform you can read
breakdown: The identity won a One Show Gold Pencil in 2021 and TDC Best in Show: a variable serif whose letters change form with the music, the reference case for audio-reactive brand type. It works because the sound is shown by the letters themselves, so the name and the music are one image. To use it: hang all letters from a shared top line, give each its own vertical scale (transform-origin at the top, or a variable-font height axis), and drive the scales from the audio spectrum or a travelling wave, easing between targets so the word stays readable at every moment.

title: The Fallen of World War II
take: Tiny figure icons stack into a column so tall the camera has to climb to find its top
breakdown: Gold winner at the Information is Beautiful Awards 2015 and the reference for cinematic unit charts: one small figure stands for a thousand people, columns are built from them, and one column outgrows the frame (around 5:40–6:10). It works because scale is felt in time: the camera has to travel to find the top. To use it: build bars from identical unit icons filling row by row, let ordinary columns stop inside the frame, and for the big one keep filling while the camera pans up at steady speed, with a counter running, before pulling back to compare.

title: Wind Map
take: Thousands of fading streaks trace an invisible flow field, brighter where it is faster
breakdown: The first web artwork in MoMA's permanent collection (2012) and the ancestor of every wind, ocean and flow visualisation since. It works because no arrows are drawn: thousands of short-lived particles follow the field and their fading trails add up to the shape of the flow. To use it: define a smooth vector field, advance a few thousand particles along it each frame, draw a short segment per step and fade the whole canvas slightly instead of clearing it, respawn particles at random after a short life, and tie brightness or length to speed.

title: RSA Animate — Drive
techniques: marker line with a single accent colour
take: Marker drawings ink in stroke by stroke as the view slides across one big sheet
breakdown: The breakout film (2010) of the series that established whiteboard animation as an explainer genre: black marker with red accents on white, the frame travelling over one continuous drawing in step with the talk. It works because the drawing is always being made, so attention stays on the newest line, and the single sheet keeps every earlier idea within reach. To use it: prepare one wide illustration as paths, reveal them in drawing order with stroke-dashoffset so a line is always in progress, pan steadily toward the newest part, and reserve one accent colour for emphasis.

title: Netflix — Logo Animation (2019)
take: Push into a flat letter until its stroke splits into a curtain of coloured light strands
breakdown: The four-second ident that has opened every Netflix original since February 2019, among the most-seen logo animations anywhere. It works because a flat mark turns out to have an inside: the camera accelerates into one stroke and the solid colour resolves into many thin vertical strands of different colours. To use it: hold a simple flat letter, scale it up with a strong ease-in around one of its strokes, and as that stroke fills the frame cross-fade it into dozens of thin vertical lines of varied hue and brightness that stretch past the frame edges; cut on the brightest moment.

title: You Can't Stop Us
take: Two clips share one frame: the motion in the left half continues in the right
breakdown: The reference for the split-screen match, winner of the 2021 Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Commercial and a Cannes Lions Film Grand Prix: every shot is two unrelated sports clips joined at a centre seam so that one movement reads as a single body (72 clips as 36 pairs). It works because the eye follows motion, not background, so a matched pose across the seam fuses two worlds. To use it: choose pairs by pose and direction of travel, align scale and horizon at the seam, cut both halves at the same instant, and let backgrounds clash on purpose.

title: Jaws — the beach scene
by: Steven Spielberg, edited by Verna Fields
take: A passer-by crossing the lens hides each cut to a tighter shot of the watcher
breakdown: The textbook wipe-by cut, from the film that won Verna Fields the Academy Award for Film Editing: while the police chief watches the water, people walk past the lens, and behind each of them the framing jumps closer to his face. It works because the cut is hidden by something that belongs to the scene, so tension tightens without the audience noticing the edit. To use it: shoot the same subject at three sizes on one axis, and place each cut on the frames where a foreground figure fully covers the subject; keep the crossings fast (about a quarter of a second).

title: The Man Your Man Could Smell Like
take: One unbroken take: the presenter holds the frame while the set swaps around him
breakdown: The canonical one-take ad, winner of the Cannes Lions Film Grand Prix and the Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Commercial in 2010: the presenter speaks to camera without a cut while the bathroom becomes a boat and then a beach. It works because the fixed subject is the anchor: with no cut to reset attention, every change of world lands as a surprise. To use it: keep the subject locked in position and eyeline, and change everything else in layers — walls lift, floors slide, props drop into the hand — one move at a time, each finishing before the next line.

title: The Civil War: The Gettysburg Address
take: Drift slowly across a still photo and push in until one face fills the frame
breakdown: The technique carries this filmmaker's name: The Civil War (1990) made slow moves across still photographs a documentary standard, and Apple later licensed 'Ken Burns Effect' for iMovie. It works because the move directs the reading of a picture: start on the group, end on one person, and a still becomes a sentence. To use it: pick a start and an end crop inside a high-resolution image, move between them at constant speed with no easing and no rotation over several seconds, and end exactly as the narration names the subject; dissolve to the next still.

title: $456,000 Squid Game In Real Life!
take: Pin a stakes HUD: a state light, a countdown clock and an N REMAINING tally
breakdown: One of the most-watched videos on YouTube (reported as the fastest non-music video to 100 million views). In its game sections the score never leaves the screen: a green/red light, a countdown and a count of players remaining stay pinned while the shots change underneath. It works because every cut updates a number the viewer is already tracking, so there is always a reason to watch the next ten seconds. To use it: decide the two or three numbers that are the stakes, pin them in fixed corners in a heavy, legible face, change them only on events, and punch the changed number briefly.

title: #1 Productivity Hack
take: Burn in captions 1–3 words at a time at chest height, key word heavier
breakdown: The caption style that carries his name in editing tools and tutorials: bold burned-in captions that appear one to three words at a time, in step with speech, with the key word emphasised (this is a recent representative short from his channel). It works because the eye never has a full sentence to skim ahead, so reading is paced by the voice and holds attention through a locked-off shot. To use it: chunk the transcript into 1–3 word groups on word timestamps, swap chunks with a tiny pop, keep them on one line at chest height clear of the face, and make one word per sentence heavier or tinted.

title: China is erasing its border with Hong Kong
take: Draw the border as a red line on a paper map, then label both sides and the date
breakdown: The most-viewed episode of the series that set the look of the modern map explainer (Vox Borders was nominated at the 39th News & Documentary Emmys). Around 0:35–1:25 the border is drawn in red, both sides get a label and a date is stamped on. It works because the map is built in the order of the argument: line first, then names, then when. To use it: put a paper texture under simple land shapes, draw the line with a stroke that animates along its path, pop a label on each side, stamp the date last, and keep a slow push-in running the whole time.

title: 1 Second Everyday — Age 30
take: One second per day: a hard cut every 1.0 s with the date stamped in the corner
breakdown: The originator of the one-second-a-day format, premiered in his TED2012 talk and later an app: a year as 365 one-second shots in strict order, each with its date in the corner. It works because the rule is the whole edit: a metronomic cut rate makes unrelated shots feel like one life, and the date turns the cut into a calendar. To use it: give every shot exactly the same length, keep hard cuts only, keep chronology, stamp a small date or counter in the same corner on every shot, and let the content, not the editing, vary.

title: I promise it works
take: Show the over-complicated hack, then cut to a silent one-move fix and a shrug
breakdown: The wordless reply format that made him the most-followed person on TikTok (Guinness World Records, 2022): someone else's over-complicated hack in busy handheld close-ups, then a locked-off shot of the obvious fix and an open-handed gesture. It works without sound or language because the contrast is in the pictures: shaky and fussy against still and simple. To use it: give the problem several quick, cluttered shots, cut hard to one calm symmetrical frame, solve it in a single move, and hold the reaction for a beat with no text.

title: 2001: A Space Odyssey — bone to satellite
take: Cut on shape: a tumbling object becomes a same-shaped object in another world
breakdown: The most cited match cut in cinema (1968): a thrown bone, turning in the air, is replaced in one cut by an orbiting satellite of the same shape and angle, jumping millions of years. It works because shape, position and direction carry over the cut, so the mind joins two worlds that have nothing else in common. To use it: end shot A with the object isolated against a plain background, start shot B with a different object at the same size, angle and place in the frame, continue the motion's direction, and use a hard cut — no dissolve.
